narration: In an old story, Theseus walked into a labyrinth holding a ball of thread, so he could always find his way back. Depth-first search is that thread. This maze has seven [[rooms]]rooms, joined by twelve one-way [[doors]]doors. Ada will explore it from room {A}, [[thread]]unrolling a thread behind her.

Ada carries a clock. [[enter]]The first time she enters a room, she advances the clock, and writes the time on the room. That is the room's starting time, its preorder number. [[leave]]When she leaves a room for good, because every door out of it has been tried, she advances the clock again, and writes that: its finishing time, its postorder number.

At any moment, every room is in one of three states. [[n]]New: Ada has never entered it. [[a]]Active: she has entered it, but not yet left it for good. [[f]]Finished: she has left it for good. [[path]]The active rooms always form one single path, from the start to Ada. That is the thread.

[[e0]]Ada enters {A}: clock one. [[e1]]The door to {B} leads to a new room, [[e2]]so she goes: clock two. [[e3]]{B} to {D}, [[e4]]clock three. [[e5]]{D} to {E}, [[e6]]clock four. [[e7]]{E} has a door back to {B}, but {B} is still on the thread. [[e8]]{E} has no more doors, so {E} is finished: clock five. [[e9]]Back in {D}: finished, clock six. [[e10]]Back in {B}: its other door, to {E}, leads to a finished room. [[e11]]{B} is finished: clock seven.

[[e12]]Back at {A}, the next door leads to {C}, [[e13]]a new room: clock eight. [[e14]]{C} to {F}, [[e15]]nine. [[e16]]{F} has a door back to {C}, which is on the thread. [[e17]]{F} to {G}, [[e18]]ten. [[e19]]{G} has a door to {D}, a finished room, in a branch Ada already completed. [[e20]]{G} is finished: eleven. [[e21]]{F} is finished: twelve. [[e22]]Back at {C}: its door to {G} leads to a finished room. [[e23]]{C} is finished: thirteen. [[e24]]Back at {A}: the last door, to {E}, also leads to a finished room. [[e25]]{A} is finished: fourteen. The walk is over.

Read the rooms by starting time, [[pre]]{A}, {B}, {D}, {E}, {C}, {F}, {G}. That is a preorder. Read them by finishing time, [[post]]{E}, {D}, {B}, {G}, {F}, {C}, {A}. That is a postorder. [[diff]]With a different order of doors, or a different starting room, you would get different ones.

Draw each room as a bar, from its starting time to its finishing time. Any two bars are either [[nest]]nested, one inside the other, or [[apart]]completely apart. [[anc]]And one room's bar contains another's exactly when it is an ancestor in the thread tree. The bar for room {B} contains the bars for {D} and {E}.

The book says this in four equivalent ways. [[l1]]One: u is an ancestor of v in the thread tree. [[l2]]Two: u's bar contains v's bar. [[l3]]Three: when v starts, u is active. [[l4]]Four: just before u starts, there is a path from u to v through rooms that are all new. [[same]]All four mean the same thing.

Now classify the doors. When Ada tries a door from u to v, there are four cases, depending on v's state at that moment. [[t1]]If v is new, it is a tree edge. [[t2]]If v is active, it is a back edge. [[t3]]If v is finished and below u, it is a forward edge. [[t4]]If v is finished, and somewhere else, it is a cross edge.
[[go]]A tree edge: v is new, so Ada walks through, and the door joins the thread tree. {A} to {B} is a tree edge. So are five more.
[[go]]A back edge: v is active, already on the thread. {E} to {B}: {B} is on the thread, so this door loops back up it. {F} to {C} does the same. Two doors are back edges.
[[go]]A forward edge: v is finished, and it is below u. {B} to {E}: Ada already reached {E} through {D}. {C} to {G} and {A} to {E} are the same. Three doors are forward edges.
[[go]]A cross edge: v is finished, and not below u. {G} to {D}: {D} sits in a branch that Ada completed before she even entered {G}'s branch. One door is a cross edge.

What do the bars look like? [[s1]]For a tree edge, u's bar contains v's. [[s2]]For a forward edge, the same. [[s3]]For a back edge, v's bar contains u's. [[s4]]For a cross edge, v's bar is entirely before u's. [[none]]A fifth kind, with v starting after u has finished, is impossible, because Ada tries every door out of u before she leaves it.

Here is the key fact. If any door leads to an active room, the maze has a cycle. [[loop]]The thread runs from {B} down to {E}, and the door from {E} back to {B} closes the loop. [[fin]]But doors to finished rooms never prove a cycle.

There is a second way to see it, with finishing times. [[tab]]Here is every door, with the two finishing times. For a back edge, the room it points to is still active when u finishes, so it finishes later. [[rule]]If an edge u to v has u finishing before v, there is a cycle. In a DAG, every edge has u finishing after v.
Now the algorithm, in Python. It keeps a status for every room. [[d]]First, an empty dictionary. [[n]]A loop sets every room's status to new.
[[a]]Visit is a function inside a function, one call per room. [[b]]The moment Ada enters v, its status becomes active. [[c]]Then, for each door out of v, to a room w, look at w's status.

[[a]]If w is active, that is a back edge. [[b]]Return False: there is a cycle. [[c]]If w is new, that is a tree edge, so [[d]]visit it. And if that visit comes back False, a cycle was found deeper down, [[e]]so return False too. If w is finished, do nothing: it can never prove a cycle.
[[a]]When every door out of v has been tried, v becomes finished. [[b]]And visit returns True: no cycle was found at or below this room.

The outer loop. [[a]]Try every room as a starting point. [[b]]Skip the ones an earlier walk already covered. [[c]]If any walk finds a cycle, the answer is False. [[d]]If every room is covered and no back edge was found, return True: the graph is a DAG.

Run it on the maze. [[go]]Visit {A}: active. Visit {B}. Visit {D}. Visit {E}. Now {E}'s door leads to {B}, and {B}'s status is active. Return False, right away: the maze has a cycle. It never even looks at the rest.

[[rm]]Remove the two back edges, {E} to {B} and {F} to {C}. Ten doors are left. [[true]]Now no door ever leads to an active room, and the function returns True. This is a DAG. [[src]]A room with no doors in is a source: here, room {A}. [[snk]]A room with no doors out is a sink: here, room {E}. [[every]]Every DAG has at least one source and one sink.

One more detail. If we start a walk from every room in turn, skipping the ones already entered, the number of separate trees depends on the order. [[one]]Start at {A}: one tree. [[two]]Start at {G} first, and the first walk is stuck after {G}, {D}, {E}, {B}. Then {A} starts a second tree. [[any]]In a directed graph, even a connected one, the count can be anything from one to V.

To recap. [[c1]]Every room gets two stamps from one clock. [[c2]]Every room is new, active, or finished, and the active rooms are the thread. [[c3]]Every door is a tree, forward, back, or cross edge. [[c4]]A back edge, an edge to an active room, means a cycle. [[next]]Next: topological sort, and dynamic programming, sections six point three and six point four.
